The agent operating model — roles, grants and supervision
blocks.sub: Staffing discipline applied to software: explicit duties, bounded tools, inspected work

blocks.x: Agentic Process Automation is delivered by an Achala practice team that stays through industrialization. Achala builds this as production infrastructure, not a pilot: every agent is versioned, every permission is scoped, every handoff to a person is logged. The result is automation your operations and compliance teams can both stand behind. Who this is for: COOs and operations leads carrying process cost, and the risk officers who must approve what the agents touch.

The build discipline is boring by design: each agent's permissions are the minimum that lets it do its role, its actions are idempotent, its retries are bounded, and every decision it makes can be replayed from the trace. Agents that fail these tests do not graduate from staging.
Below: the failure modes that make agent programs fragile, the reference architecture that makes them defensible, and the console that shows exactly what the digital staff did today.

widgets.title: Anatomy of one governed run — click each stage

stages.name: Goal intake
stages.detail: The run starts as a typed request object — goal, constraints, deadline, budget class — not a free-text prompt. Typed intake is what makes replay and cost accounting possible.

stages.name: Plan
stages.detail: Planner emits a step graph with tool candidates per node; the policy layer strikes any tool the credentials of this run class cannot touch, before execution begins.

stages.name: Execute
stages.detail: Every write carries an idempotency key; every read is cached by content hash. Retries are budgeted — the third retry of the same call escalates instead.

stages.name: Verify
stages.detail: Critic asserts output shape and business checks (totals reconcile, dates in range); the policy gate re-checks scope before any side effect lands.

stages.name: Ledger
stages.detail: Inputs, plan revisions, tool I/O, model versions and cost are sealed into the run record — the artifact an auditor or incident review reads first.

widgets.note: The five stages are the same for a $0.10 data-entry run and a $4 exception run — only the budgets differ.

Idempotency is the load-bearing wall
blocks.sub: The engineering property every agent action inherits, and what we build when a system cannot offer it

blocks.x: Every write an agent makes carries an idempotency key, and the key is semantic, not syntactic: two calls that would move the same business object to the same state share a key, so a retry after timeout cannot double-book, double-pay or double-file. Systems that support idempotent writes natively get used directly; systems that do not get a reconciliation shim that proves the intended end-state before the run is allowed to close. This is why our failure rate claims survive audit, a run that could not prove its end-state is a failed run by definition, and the failure is visible in the run ledger, not in a spreadsheet.

The second wall is the retry budget. Agents do not retry until success; they retry within a budget, bounded attempts, bounded cost, bounded wall-clock, and when the budget exhausts, the run escalates with its trace attached. The economics matter: an agent that retries expensive LLM calls until the bill spikes is the most common cost failure we inherit from prior programs. The circuit breaker on spend is set at design time from the risk matrix, reviewed at every release gate, and it trips loudly when it trips.

items: Semantic idempotency keys
Same business object + same end-state = same key; retries collapse, side effects stay single.
Reconciliation shims
For systems without native idempotency, end-state is proven from source before a run closes.
Budgeted retries
Bounded attempts, cost and wall-clock; exhaustion escalates with trace attached.
Spend circuit breakers
Per-run and per-cohort ceilings from the risk matrix; trips are loud and reviewed at gates.

items: How do you prevent agents from taking destructive actions in production systems?

Every tool grant is role-scoped, typed and expiring; destructive verbs either require a checkpoint approval or are simply not in the grant. Replay coverage is 100%, so any action can be re-executed step by step under audit.
What happens when an agent hits a case it cannot handle?

A confidence or policy failure routes the case to a human queue with the evidence packet attached, the agent never improvises an exception path. The escalation reason is logged and becomes calibration data for the next cohort.
Can this run against our existing ERP and CRM, or do we need new infrastructure?

Agents integrate through typed contracts against your existing ERP, CRM and ITSM, no parallel estate. The integration surface is named system by system in the engagement, with rate limits and idempotency keys on every seam.
How is agent cost controlled as volume grows?
Each process family carries a unit-cost target and a per-run ceiling; the console shows cost against ceiling in real time, and a breached ceiling pages the process owner before the invoice does.
Who owns the agent after go-live — us or you?

Your process owner holds the runbooks, consoles and re-certification calendar from week one. We operate alongside until the cohort passes its stability window, then step back to an advisory retainer if you want one.
